A_target.statement:
Let $q \in \Bbb H$ be a [[Definition:Unit Quaternion|unit quaternion]].
Then:
:$\mathbf v \mapsto q \mathbf v q^{-1}$
is a [[Definition:Rotation (Geometry)|rotation]] of $\R^3$, identified with the purely imaginary quaternions, and $q$ and $-q$ give the same rotation.

B_source.statement:
Let $z \in \C$ with $\size z = 1$.
Then $w \mapsto z w$ is a [[Definition:Rotation (Geometry)|rotation]] of $\R^2 \cong \C$.

substitutions.the plane acted upon: the purely imaginary quaternions, a three-dimensional space

derived.the norm being multiplicative: the same, so conjugation preserves length
derived.the correspondence being one-to-one: a two-to-one correspondence, since q and -q act identically

object_map.reformulation: Replace multiplication by conjugation so that noncommutativity is absorbed and the imaginary subspace is preserved.

validity_conditions: The quaternion norm is multiplicative, so conjugation by a unit quaternion preserves length and is therefore an orthogonal transformation.

Multiplication alone does not work because quaternions are noncommutative and left multiplication does not preserve the purely imaginary subspace; conjugation is the correct replacement and does preserve it.
The map from unit quaternions to rotations is two-to-one rather than injective, since q and -q induce the same conjugation, which is the essential departure from the complex case.
proof_plan: Identify $\R^3$ with the purely imaginary quaternions $\set {x i + y j + z k}$.

Replace multiplication by conjugation $\map {R_q} {\mathbf v} = q \mathbf v q^{-1}$.
As $\map {\operatorname {Re} } {q \mathbf v q^{-1} } = \map {\operatorname {Re} } {\mathbf v} = 0$, conjugation preserves the imaginary subspace.

By multiplicativity of the [[Definition:Norm of Quaternion|norm]], $\norm {\map {R_q} {\mathbf v} } = \norm {\mathbf v}$, so $R_q$ is [[Definition:Orthogonal Transformation|orthogonal]].
As the unit quaternions form a [[Definition:Connected Space|connected]] set and $R_1 = I$, $\map \det {R_q} = 1$.
